Title: How to Prevent Plantar Fasciitis
Author: Michael Greger M.D. FACLM
Description: If plantar fasciitis is an overuse injury where damage outpaces repair, how can we reduce microtrauma and also facilitate healing?
Transcript:
Below is an approximation of this video’s audio content. To see any graphs, charts, graphics, images, and quotes to which Dr. Greger may be referring, watch the above video.
The most accepted theory for the cause of plantar fasciitis presents it as an overuse injury in which the rate of damage from repetitive microtrauma exceeds the body’s healing capacity. Stress on the plantar fascia can be reduced by avoiding excess body weight, prolonged standing, and excessive running. Those who are obese have five to six times the odds of plantar fasciitis compared to those who are not. Individuals with occupations requiring them to stand have three to four times the odds, and up to one in six runners is affected.
Those with plantar fasciitis are recommended to avoid flat, unsupportive shoes, such as flip-flops. In the past, running barefoot was recommended as a treatment for plantar fasciitis, but subsequent evidence suggests that being barefoot may do more harm than good, possibly even increasing the risk of developing the condition in the first place.
Plantar fasciitis is one of the reasons runners are urged to regularly replace their running shoes. Is that just overpriced shoe company propaganda? Those with a rearfoot strike pattern (by far the most common) have about a 15 to 30 percent reduction in the amount of heel cushioning after running about 300 miles, though even experienced recreational runners don’t perceive these changes even after running 400 miles. It’s unclear if this difference is enough to make an actual difference. A study of runners found, paradoxically, that running in new shoes was associated with both decreased and increased rates of injury. Perhaps the apparent protection from the new shoes came from greater cushioning and support, whereas the apparent risk of injury was reverse causation. (Rather than the new running shoes preventing injury, injured runners were trying to solve their issues with frequent shoe changes.) Special “double air-cushioned” shoes were put to the test for plantar fasciitis and failed to significantly improve symptoms.
Decreasing microtrauma injury is just half of the equation. What can we do to boost healing? One thing that may negatively affect tendon healing is having a high cholesterol level. Just as excess cholesterol in our system can infiltrate our artery walls and trigger inflammation, deposition of cholesterol in our tendons leads to a persistent inflammatory state that can result in chronic tendon degeneration. This may help explain why high cholesterol is also associated with Achilles’ tendon disorders, tennis elbow, and rotator cuff tears.
Patients with Achilles’ tendon rupture are about three times as likely to have high cholesterol compared to matched controls with intact tendons. In fact, that’s one of the ways familial hypercholesterolemia is diagnosed— an ultrasound measurement of the thickness of the Achilles’ tendon. Familial hypercholesterolemia is an inherited condition that leads to extremely high cholesterol, so much so that the tendon swells with cholesterol accumulation. Having high LDL cholesterol may triple the odds of plantar fasciitis.
Animal studies prove cause-and-effect. In rats, even mildly elevated cholesterol impaired tendon-healing abilities. and when mice were fed a diet high in saturated fat, researchers found a marked increase in cholesterol deposition in their tendons, which significantly adversely affected their tendon function in terms of failure stress and the load the tendon is able to bear. Though there hasn’t been a trial of cholesterol-lowering drugs for plantar fasciitis, cholesterol-lowering therapy may be able to improve the musculoskeletal manifestations (mainly tendonitis) in the majority of those with familial hypercholesterolemia.
If you do develop plantar fasciitis, what’s the best treatment? Certain stretching exercises are so helpful in treating it they might also be helpful in preventing it in the first place. I’ll cover plantar fasciitis treatment, next.

Since plantar fasciitis is thought to be caused by an overuse injury in which the rate of damage from repetitive microtrauma exceeds the body’s healing capacity, there’s a two-fold way to prevent it: (1) Decrease microtrauma injury by avoiding excess body weight, prolonged standing, and excessive running, and, at the same time, (2) boost healing, which may involve lowering LDL cholesterol levels.
